# Diagnosing Intermittent Stalls in a 2005 Honda Accord: The TPS Connection

When a vehicle exhibits symptoms like low cold idle and stalling once warm, it often points to a mismatch between actual engine load and the commanded fuel/air mixture. In the specific case of your 2005 Honda Accord 4-cylinder, the diagnostic path taken reveals a classic example of how sensor feedback loops can mask underlying issues until environmental factors interfere.

The initial symptoms described—a cold idle dropping to approximately 500 RPM and stalling upon reaching operating temperature—suggest the engine control unit (ECU) was losing confidence in its ability to maintain stable combustion as thermal expansion altered clearances or airflow dynamics. The systematic troubleshooting performed, including cleaning battery terminals, inspecting the air filter, and bypassing the Mass Airflow Sensor (MAF), is a logical approach for isolating intake and power delivery issues. However, several of these steps are essentially software resets or mechanical adjustments that rarely resolve deep-sensor failures.

The critical pivot point in your diagnosis occurred when disconnecting the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS). Disconnecting this sensor typically triggers a "limp mode" strategy where the ECU defaults to a fixed wide-open throttle map, often resulting in a higher, more stable idle because it ignores minor fluctuations in throttle plate position. The fact that the engine ran fine with the TPS disconnected but failed immediately upon reconnection confirms the root cause was electrical or mechanical within the sensor circuit itself.

It is important to understand why connecting the TPS caused the check engine light (CEL) to illuminate immediately. Modern ECUs perform continuous plausibility checks on sensor inputs. If the voltage signal from the TPS falls outside a predefined range, shows an invalid slope change during acceleration, or exhibits noise, the ECU stores a fault code and illuminates the MIL (Malfunction Indicator Lamp). When you filled the tank at the gas station, the fuel system reset may have cleared volatile memory flags or provided enough ethanol-free gasoline to temporarily smooth combustion, allowing the CEL to turn off. However, if the TPS hardware remains faulty, the engine will likely revert to a rough idle or stall once the ECU re-evaluates the sensor data under load.

To prevent recurrence, you should not rely on driving through the symptom but rather replace the TPS assembly. On many GM and older Honda platforms, these are inexpensive components that wear out due to carbon buildup on the potentiometer inside the housing. Before replacing it, verify the resistance values across the three wires (reference voltage, ground, and signal) while gently moving the throttle from closed to open; a smooth linear increase in voltage indicates health, whereas a jump or drop indicates failure.

Additionally, consider the Idle Air Control Valve (IACV). While you attempted to clean it via tapping with a screwdriver, carbon deposits often harden into a crust that prevents proper valve travel even if the motor spins freely. Cleaning the IACV body and its seat with carburetor cleaner, followed by a relearn procedure where the car is driven until the radiator fan cycles on two or three times, can sometimes restore baseline idle behavior independent of the TPS issue.

If you are looking for structured diagnostic workflows to reference in the future, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) often compile community-driven troubleshooting guides that break down these specific sensor interactions into reproducible steps for other technicians facing similar legacy vehicle challenges.
